t: Line Reflection — Hash Set on the Mirror Axis
o: We must decide whether some vertical line $x = c$ reflects the point set onto itself. Reflection over $x = c$ maps a point $(x, y)$ to $(2c - x, y)$, so for every point its mirror partner (possibly itself) must exist in the set. In Example 1, points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,1)$ mirror across $x = 0$, so the answer is true. In Example 2, $(1,1)$ would need a partner at $(-1,1)$, which is absent, so no vertical line works and the answer is false. With $n$ up to $10^4$, an $O(n^2)$ pairwise check is borderline but an $O(n)$ hash-set solution is clearly preferred.
k: Reflection over a vertical line $x = c$ sends $(x, y) \to (2c - x, y)$; only the x-coordinate changes, so points pair up by equal y.
If a reflecting line exists, it must lie exactly halfway between the minimum and maximum x-coordinates, so $c = (\min_x + \max_x)/2$ is forced.
Storing all points in a set lets us verify each point's mirror in $O(1)$ average time, giving an overall linear algorithm.

a.i: Try every candidate axis of symmetry defined by pairing point $i$ with point $j$: the axis is $x = (x_i + x_j)/2$. For each candidate axis, verify that every point's reflection exists among the points by scanning all points. This directly mirrors the definition of symmetry and needs no cleverness, but costs quadratic time.
s: For each pair of points $(i, j)$, compute the candidate axis $c = (x_i + x_j)/2$.
For each candidate axis, check every point $p$: confirm that $(2c - p.x, p.y)$ exists somewhere in the input.
If all checks pass for any axis, return true; otherwise return false after trying all pairs.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case — up to O(n^2) candidate axes, each verified in O(n).
a.sp: O(n) for the deduplicated point storage.

a.i: The axis of symmetry, if it exists, must be exactly midway between the smallest and largest x-coordinates, since those extreme points must reflect onto each other. So we do not search for the axis — we compute it. Then we put all points into a hash set and check that each point's mirror $(\min_x + \max_x - x, y)$ is present. Duplicates are harmless because they map to themselves and are already in the set.
s: Deduplicate points into a hash set while tracking minX and maxX.
Set the target sum S = minX + maxX (the doubled axis coordinate).
For every unique point (x, y), check whether (S - x, y) is in the set.
Return true only if every check passes.
a.t: O(n) expected — one pass to build the set and find extremes, one pass to verify mirrors (hash operations are O(1) average; using a balanced tree gives O(n log n)).
a.sp: O(n) for the set of unique points.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 2: deduplicate, compute the forced axis from min/max x, then verify mirrors with a hash set — simple, linear, and easy to explain. Common pitfalls: forgetting to deduplicate (duplicates can cause false negatives if you pop from lists instead of using a set), integer overflow when encoding coordinates as keys in Java/C++ (use 64-bit keys or pairs), and assuming the axis could be anything other than (minX + maxX)/2. Edge cases: a single point (always true), all points identical (true), and points symmetric about a non-zero axis like x = 5. Likely follow-ups: handle a diagonal axis of symmetry (rotate coordinates first), or return the axis itself instead of a boolean.
